abstract.text: Background: Vitamin D supplementation may reduce respiratory infections in older adults. Methods: We randomised 412 participants aged 65–85 years. Results: Infections fell by 18% (95% CI 6–29). Conclusions: Supplementation was associated with fewer infections.

methods.text: We conducted a double‑blind, placebo‑controlled randomised trial in 12 primary care clinics between 2019 and 2022. Participants aged 65–85 years were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive 50 µg of vitamin D3 daily or a matching placebo for 12 months. Participants were asked to avoid “over‑the‑counter” supplements during the trial. The primary outcome was the number of acute respiratory infections confirmed by a clinician. Allocation was concealed using a central web‑based system, and participants, clinicians and outcome assessors were masked to group assignment. The sample size of 412 participants provided 80% power to detect a 20% relative reduction at a two‑sided α of 0.05.

results.text: Of 498 people screened, 412 were randomised and 389 (94%) completed follow‑up. The mean age was 72.4 years (SD 5.1), and 231 (56%) participants were women. Acute respiratory infections occurred in 81 participants in the vitamin D group and 99 in the placebo group (risk ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.94; p=0.004). Hospital admissions did not differ between groups (14 vs 17; p=0.58). Serum 25‑hydroxyvitamin D increased from 42 to 78 nmol/L in the intervention group. No serious adverse events were attributed to the intervention, although mild hypercalcaemia was reported in 3 participants.

discussion.text: In this trial, daily vitamin D3 reduced the risk of clinician‑confirmed respiratory infections by about 18%. The effect was not explained by differences in influenza vaccination, which was similar in both groups. These ﬁndings are consistent with earlier meta‑analyses but contrast with trials that used large monthly bolus doses. Our study was not powered to detect differences in hospital admissions.

conclusions.text: Daily vitamin D3 supple­mentation was associated with fewer respiratory infections in older adults living in the community. It did not reduce hospital admissions. Further trials should test whether the benefit persists beyond 12 months.
